What We Learned

  1. Increasing multiplicative functions are completely multiplicative.
    Monotonicity can strengthen multiplicativity: for a increasing multiplicative arithmetic function, the identity extends from coprime positive integers to all positive integers.

  2. Infimum and supremum arguments can establish exact identities.
    By comparing nearby integers and exploiting multiplicativity, we can derive upper and lower bounds for ratios of function values. When these bounds coincide, an exact identity follows.

  3. The density of rational numbers can compare growth rates.
    Rational approximation allows us to compare integer powers and derive contradictions when the logarithmic growth exponents of a completely multiplicative function differ.

  4. Decreasing multiplicative functions behave differently.
    Unlike increasing multiplicative functions, decreasing multiplicative functions need not be completely multiplicative. They may vanish at every integer greater than or equal to .

  5. Bertrand-Chebyshev theorem connects multiplicativity with monotonicity.
    The existence of a prime between and provides inequalities relating function values at consecutive primes. These inequalities can be combined with induction to establish positivity properties.
